title: Wafer & yield
summary: Why defects make big dies expensive, and why chiplets help.

challenges.title: Fill the shelf
challenges.task: Rain ruins every chip it hits. Make twice as many working chips from the same wafer.
challenges.hint: Cut the chips smaller, one step at a time, and watch the shelf. The rain stays where it is.
challenges.why: A small chip dodges rain that a big one would catch, so the same drops ruin far less. Each cut still costs a little: the pieces need extra silicon to link them, and a working chip needs all its pieces.

challenges.title: Half price by chiplets
challenges.task: Split the AI GPU die until a working chip costs less than half as much silicon as one big die. What is the smallest split that does it?
challenges.hint: Start from the AI GPU die preset and try each split in turn, watching the silicon cost per chip. Half of $1,077 is about $538.
challenges.why: Yield falls exponentially with area, so a small die dodges defects far more often. But each split adds area for the links between chiplets, so the saving shrinks: 4 chiplets get you to $580, and it takes 8 to go below half.

challenges.title: The yield cliff
challenges.task: Raise the defect density on one AI GPU die until fewer than 1 in 10 dies work. How dirty is that, and what does each working chip cost then?
challenges.hint: Keep one big AI GPU die and raise the defect density slowly. Watch the model yield fall below 10%.
challenges.why: At about 0.28 defects per cm², fewer than 1 in 10 dies of this size work, and each working chip costs about $4,800 of silicon. A die this big turns a slightly dirty fab into a very expensive one, which is why new nodes start with small chips.

challenges.title: A $45,000 wafer
challenges.task: Suppose wafers at a future node cost $45,000. Keep the silicon for a working AI GPU under $1,000: how clean must the fab be for one big die, and how much dirt can 8 chiplets tolerate?
challenges.hint: Set the wafer price to $45k and keep one die. Lower the defect density until a working chip costs less than $1,000. Then try 8 chiplets.
challenges.why: One big die stays under $1,000 only while the fab is very clean, about 0.04 defects per cm² or less. Split into 8 chiplets, it stays under $1,000 even at 0.2. Dearer wafers make chiplets more attractive, not less.

challenges.title: Half price in clumps
challenges.task: Real defects clump together. With clumps on, find how loose they must be before 8 chiplets reach half price again.
challenges.hint: Start at α = 1, where the cost ratio is about 0.59, and raise α one step at a time.
challenges.why: Clumps leave gaps, so a big die survives more often than even rain suggests, and cutting saves less. At the default density, half price returns at about α = 5. The tighter the clumps, the weaker the case for chiplets on cost alone.

learn.plain: Picture raindrops falling on a tiled floor: any tile hit by a drop is ruined. Big tiles get hit more often, so cutting a design into smaller tiles (chiplets) wastes less.
learn.engineer: Common yield models are Poisson e^(−AD₀), Murphy ((1 − e^(−AD₀)) ÷ AD₀)² and negative binomial (1 + AD₀/α)^(−α), where α captures how defects cluster. Defect density falls along a learning curve as a node ramps. Redundancy (spare memory rows, fused-off cores) and binning recover partly defective dies, which is why many products ship with some units disabled.

quiz.q: What happens to yield as die area grows, at the same defect density?
options: It does not depend on area
quiz.why: Poisson yield is e^(−A·D₀): a bigger area catches more defects.

options: The largest area a scanner prints in one exposure, about 26 × 33 mm
The number of wafers per hour
quiz.why: High-NA EUV halves it to 26 × 16.5 mm, which pushes large designs toward chiplets.

quiz.q: Why can chiplets lower the cost of a working chip?
options: Smaller dies yield better, and only known-good dies are combined
quiz.why: The trade-off is extra area and cost for die-to-die links and advanced packaging.
